summary: DANE lets a domain's administrators publish in DNS which keys or certificates their TLS servers use, using the TLSA record. This reduces dependence on third-party certificate authorities and requires changes in client software but not server software.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking a stranger to vouch for a site, the site's own phone book entry lists which key to expect.

questions: what are the tlsa certificate usages
where are tlsa records stored in dns
subtitle: How a domain publishes, in DNSSEC-signed DNS, which certificate or key its TLS servers must use.

tldr.problem: TLS clients trust a large set of public certification authorities, and any one of them can issue a certificate for any domain name. A single compromised or careless CA can undermine every TLS-protected site.
tldr.mechanism: The domain administrator publishes a TLSA record in DNS, at a name built from the port and transport, saying which certificate or public key (or its hash) the server must present. A client fetches the record, checks that DNSSEC validated it, and compares it with the certificate the server sends.
tldr.outcome: A domain can pin its own certificate associations without a third-party CA, and a TLSA record is limited to its own name, protocol and port. It needs DNSSEC and changes in TLS client software, but no change in TLS server software. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 7218, RFC 7671 and RFC 8749.

today: RFC 6698 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2012. It has been updated by RFC 7218, RFC 7671 and RFC 8749, and has not been obsoleted. Read those updates together with this RFC for the current DANE TLSA rules.

sections.title: Why DANE Exists
sections.content:
TLS protects traffic with encryption, but encryption is only as good as the keys. TLS binds keys to names with certificates, and clients check them against a set of trust anchors, the keys of public Certification Authorities (CAs). The RFC points out the weakness: the public CA model lets any of these CAs issue a certificate for any domain name, so one CA that betrays its trust or protects its secrets poorly can undermine the security of every certificate.

DANE (DNS-Based Authentication of Named Entities) uses DNSSEC to store and sign the keys and certificates that TLS uses. In DNSSEC the keys for a name can only be signed by the parent zone: the keys for example.com only by com, and those for com only by the DNS root. The RFC argues that this gives DANE the security principle of least privilege that the public CA model lacks. The protocol here is called DANE TLSA, and TLSA does not stand for anything; it is just the name of the record type.

The document covers TLS and DTLS, and only PKIX certificates. It does not specify how a client performs DNSSEC validation, only that the TLSA data must be validated. Other protocols, such as IPsec and SSH keys, are handled in other documents.
sections.eli5: Today your browser trusts lots of strangers to say which key belongs to a website, and one dishonest stranger can cause trouble. DANE lets the website owner say it themselves in a record nobody can fake.

sections.title: The TLSA Record
sections.content:
A TLSA resource record ties a TLS server certificate or public key to the domain name where the record is found, forming a TLSA certificate association. The record has three one-octet fields followed by the certificate association data: certificate usage, selector and matching type.

The selector says which part of the server certificate is matched: 0 is the full certificate and 1 is the SubjectPublicKeyInfo. The matching type says how the data is presented: 0 is an exact match on the selected content, 1 is a SHA-256 hash and 2 is a SHA-512 hash. The association data is either the raw selected bytes (matching type 0) or their hash (types 1 and 2).

In a zone file the three fields are written as 8-bit unsigned integers and the association data as hexadecimal characters, where whitespace is allowed. The record is class independent and has no special TTL requirements.

The certificate usages apply only to PKIX certificates in DER encoding. Any other certificate format would need its own usage values.
sections.eli5: A TLSA record is a little card with three codes and a long number. The codes say which part of the certificate to look at and whether to compare it exactly or by its fingerprint, and the number is what it has to match.

sections.title: The Four Certificate Usages
sections.content:
The certificate usage field decides how the record is used when checking the certificate the server presents.

  • 0, CA constraint: a CA certificate (or its public key) that MUST appear in a PKIX certification path for the server's end entity certificate. The presented certificate MUST also pass normal PKIX path validation. This limits which CA can issue for the service.
  • 1, service certificate constraint: the end entity certificate itself. It MUST match the record and MUST pass PKIX path validation.
  • 2, trust anchor assertion: a certificate that MUST be used as the trust anchor when validating the server's certificate. It lets a domain use its own CA that clients do not already trust. The server SHOULD send the referenced certificate just as it sends intermediate certificates.
  • 3, domain-issued certificate: the end entity certificate, which MUST match the record. PKIX validation is not tested, so the domain can issue certificates without a third-party CA.
sections.eli5: There are four ways to use the card. It can say which certificate company you may use, which exact certificate to use, which company to treat as boss, or just which certificate the website must show with no company needed.

sections.title: Where TLSA Records Live
sections.content:
TLSA records are stored at a prefixed name. The left-most label is an underscore followed by the decimal port number, with no leading zeros. The second label is an underscore followed by the transport name, which can be tcp, udp or sctp. The fully qualified name of the TLS server is appended, and every label MUST follow the host name rules of RFC 952. Internationalized names MUST use the A-label form.

So a TLSA record for an HTTP server on port 443 at www.example.com is looked up at _443._tcp.www.example.com, and one for an SMTP server using STARTTLS on port 25 at mail.example.com is looked up at _25._tcp.mail.example.com. Because the port is part of the name, different services on one host can have different records.
sections.eli5: The card is filed in a drawer labelled with the door number and the kind of road, so the client knows exactly where to look for the right one.

sections.title: How a Client Uses TLSA Records
sections.content:
A client queries for TLSA records and validates them with DNSSEC. What it does next depends on the DNSSEC validation state of the answer.

  • Secure: the records MUST be used, unless local policy prohibits a specific association.
  • Bogus: TLS MUST NOT start, or the connection MUST be aborted if negotiation is already in progress.
  • Indeterminate or insecure: the records cannot be used and are unusable, so TLS proceeds in the normal way.

An association with a usage, selector or matching type the client does not understand, with malformed data, or with an algorithm too weak for the client's policy MUST be considered unusable. If zero usable associations remain, TLS is processed normally. If there are one or more, the client tries each against the server's end entity certificate until one matches. If none match, the client MUST abort the handshake.

The session MUST be for the same port and transport named in the TLSA query. The lookup can happen before the handshake or during it. Clients that rely on another entity to validate DNSSEC MUST use a secure mechanism to reach it, such as TSIG, SIG(0) or IPsec; a secure link to a resolver that does not validate is not enough. Section 6 requires clients to handle usages 0 to 3, selectors 0 and 1, and matching types 0 and 1, and to SHOULD handle matching type 2.
sections.eli5: The client looks up the card and checks the seal. A broken seal means stop. No card, or a card it cannot read, means carry on as usual. A good card means the website's certificate has to match it, or the client leaves.

sections.title: Deploying TLSA Records
sections.content:
Appendix A warns that a secure TLSA RRset effectively disables other forms of name and path validation, so a misconfigured record locks out all conforming clients, and the document offers no way to move to TLSA gradually.

Choosing a selector matters for usages 0 and 2. Clients may build their own certificate chains, so a full-certificate association (selector 0) can fail if a client swaps in a reissued or cross-certificate. A SubjectPublicKeyInfo association (selector 1) avoids that kind of failure, but it widens the attack surface because any CA could later issue a certificate with the same public key. Unless the administrator understands the implications for a certificate above the directly signing CA, the RFC says selector 0 is the better option from a security perspective.

TLSA records behave like any other record type with prefixed labels. A CNAME can redirect the prefixed name to a target domain, a DNAME can alias a subtree such as _tcp, and a wildcard such as *._tcp.www.example.com can cover every TCP port of a host. Certificate rollover follows the pre-publish method: add the new record next to the old one, wait for it to propagate and for the old record's TTL to expire, switch the server to the new certificate, then remove the old record.
sections.eli5: If you write the card wrong, nobody can get in, so be careful. When you change keys, put the new card in next to the old one, wait until everyone has seen it, switch keys, and only then throw the old card away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of TLSA rests on DNSSEC. If the authentication for changing TLSA data in a zone is weaker than that for changing A and AAAA records, a man-in-the-middle who can use the weaker path may be able to impersonate the host. The RFC recommends the same level of authentication for all changes to a name.

Compared to public CAs, a DNSKEY can only sign records for its own zone, so a compromise of the key for example.com gives no route to attack example.org, and only a compromise of the root DNSKEY equals an unconstrained public CA. The RFC also notes that neither model prevents a near-invisible attack when the necessary keys are compromised, and that DANE can bypass the checks some CAs use against look-alike domain names.

A TLSA record with usage 2 can override the revocation of a certificate, because the client treats it as a trust anchor and does not check its revocation status. It can also let an intermediate CA become a trust anchor and escape policy restrictions. SSL proxies that substitute their own certificate will not work with TLSA records. Implementations that cache lookups MUST observe the TTL. DNSSEC validation is best performed on the host, because an external validator or the AD flag can be spoofed or compromised.
sections.eli5: The card is only as safe as the seal on it, so the lock on the phone book must be as strong as the lock on the address entries. And a card that makes a company the boss can hide a company that was banned.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The TLSA RR type value is 52, allocated from the DNS Resource Record TYPEs subregistry. The RFC creates three new registries: TLSA Certificate Usages (policy RFC Required), TLSA Selectors and TLSA Matching Types (both Specification Required). In each, value 255 is for private use, and the usages 0 to 3, selectors 0 and 1 and matching types 0 to 2 are the initial entries.
sections.eli5: The record type got its own number, and three lists were started so that new kinds of cards can be added later in an orderly way.

items.label: CA constraint
items.desc: A CA certificate that must appear in a valid PKIX path.

items.label: Service certificate constraint
items.desc: The end entity certificate; must also pass PKIX validation.

items.label: Trust anchor assertion
items.desc: A certificate used as the trust anchor for validation.

items.label: Domain-issued certificate
items.desc: The end entity certificate; PKIX validation is not tested.
